summary: A proposal for a reconnection protocol, so one or both ends of a connection can move to another host. It gives examples such as TIP users using an executive program on a bigger host, presents a mechanism, sketches how it fits Host-Host or Telnet, and suggests where it belongs.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC proposes a way to redirect a communication path from one host to another. It describes how the two sides agree to the move, handle competing requests and fit the feature into Host-Host or TELNET.

questions: moving a network connection to another host
how does the reconnection protocol work
how can a connection move to another host
how does rfc 426 handle simultaneous reconnect requests
subtitle: A proposed method for moving one or both ends of a connection to another host.

tldr.problem: A user or process may need to move a communication path to another host without exposing the handoff to the user.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal uses Reconnect Request, OK, No and Do commands to negotiate and redirect a path, with rules for simultaneous requests.
tldr.outcome: The author recommends adding reconnection as an optional TELNET feature for pragmatic reasons, while noting that Host-Host support would be more general.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 426 as Unknown and records no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. The document presents a reconnection proposal and recommends an optional TELNET approach.

sections.title: When Reconnection Helps
sections.content:
The RFC gives three examples. A TIP user could start at an executive program on one host and then be handed to another host for work. A host could hand a user to an authentication service and then back to the requested host. A distributed simulation could move a program component to another computer and reconnect its neighbors.

In each case, the aim is to move a communication path while making the transition invisible to the user when appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: A user or program may need to move to a different host while continuing its work. The examples include an executive program, an authentication service and a distributed simulation.

sections.title: Reconnect Commands
sections.content:
The mechanism defines Reconnect Request (RRQ), Reconnect OK (ROK), Reconnect No (RNO) and Reconnect Do (RDO). One host asks the other to redirect a path; the other can accept or refuse; after acceptance, the requester specifies the new destination and the old path is broken.

The requester must arrange for the new destination to cooperate. Either side can refuse or abort. Receipt of ROK indicates that no further messages are coming from the agreeing side, and receipt of RDO indicates that no further messages are coming from the requester.
sections.plainLanguage: One host requests a move, the other accepts or refuses, and the requester identifies the new destination. The hosts coordinate the change so that the old path can close and a new one can open.

sections.title: Simultaneous Requests
sections.content:
If adjacent entities request reconnection at the same time, the RFC says to resolve the requests in series rather than in parallel. The suggested ordering compares a 40-bit value formed from a 32-bit socket number and an 8-bit site address.

The entity with the larger value proceeds first. Once an order is established, reconnection continues as if there had been no conflict.
sections.plainLanguage: If both ends request a move at once, they compare identifiers to decide who proceeds first. The other request can then be handled in order.

sections.title: Host-Host or TELNET
sections.content:
The RFC sketches adding the commands directly to Host-Host protocol or adding them to TELNET. Host-Host support would make reconnection available to higher-level protocols, but would require NCP rewrites.

For pragmatic reasons, the author recommends a TELNET option using prepare, begin-by-sending and begin-by-waiting commands. The RFC also says local entities should be able to control how remotely initiated requests are handled, including transparent, visible, confirmation and rejection modes.
sections.plainLanguage: Host-Host support would make reconnection more widely available but require NCP changes. The author therefore recommends an optional TELNET feature and says users should have control over incoming requests.
